changelog: First public release of fx-hud — Miami Neon, all-in-one FiveM HUD (QBCore / ESX / QBox / Standalone).
The weapon widget now shows the item picture and the item label from your inventory instead of the generic weapon drawing, so a pistol looks like the pistol your players see in their bag.

The image folder is found on its own, no setup needed: tgiann-inventory (inventory_images/images), ox_inventory (read from the inventory:imagepath convar, so a moved folder or a CDN still works), qb-inventory, qs-inventory, lj-inventory, ps-inventory (html/images) and codem-inventory (html/itemimages). Anything else can be added as one line under Config.Weapon.imageSources.

Mixed .png and .webp item pictures in the same inventory are handled. Both extensions are tried and the first one that loads wins; the working folder and extension are then remembered, so switching weapons does not retry the misses. If an item has no picture at all, the built-in drawing stays — the widget never shows a broken image.

The label follows the same rule: it is read from ox_inventory or from your shared items list, so a renamed weapon item reads the same in the HUD as it does in the inventory. Custom weapons your framework knows about are picked up automatically.

New console command /fxweaponimg prints the detected image folder, the resolved item name and every URL that was tried for the weapon in hand. Use it if a picture does not appear — it tells you whether the folder, the item name or the file itself is the problem.

The ammo counter now reads magazine / spare instead of magazine / total. A freshly loaded pistol used to read 12 / 12 because the game counts the rounds in the magazine as part of the total; it now reads 12 / 0 and the spare count drops as magazines are used. The bar under the counter follows the magazine, so it stays meaningful when the spare count reaches zero.

Ammo is now read continuously while a weapon is drawn, including while the inventory or pause menu is open, and every frame during a reload. Previously the counter froze whenever the HUD was hidden, so ammo taken from the inventory did not show up until the first shot was fired.

The weapon panel can now be moved and scaled in the layout editor like every other widget. It was missing from the editor's element list, so it could not be selected at all and stayed where it was when the money panel was moved, which is how it ended up sitting on top of the cash and bank rows. It is also forced visible while the editor is open, so it can be placed without drawing a weapon first.
Fixed the ammo bar stretching across the whole top-right column and drawing over the money rows. It was being positioned against that column instead of the weapon panel it belongs to.

GTA's own weapon icon and ammo counter in the top right is now hidden, so the ammo is not shown twice on screen. It is on by default and can be turned back on with the new Config.HideGtaUI.weaponAmmo setting.

The minimap no longer shows up on the character selection and loading screens. It was being switched off four times a second, which is not enough against a character selection resource that switches it back on every frame; it is now held off every frame until the player is loaded, and again after a logout.

Pressing Z no longer blows the minimap up to full screen. GTA expands the radar on that key by itself, so a keybind change was not enough; the control is now blocked every frame. Config.Minimap.bigMapKey now ships as false, and the new Config.Minimap.blockBigMapKey turns the block on and off.

UPGRADING: config.lua is escrow_ignored, so your own file is kept and will not have the new keys. Both features still work without touching it — the inventory list falls back to the built-in one, and the Z block turns itself on only if no big map key is set. To disable the Z block while keeping your key, or to add your own inventory folder, copy Config.Weapon.itemImage / imageSources and Config.Minimap.blockBigMapKey over from the new config.lua.

NEW — Config.Branding: the colours of the server name, the character name, the ID badge and the UTC stamp are now set from the config instead of the stylesheet. The flowing gradient that runs through the server name and the character name takes its colour stops, its speed and its step interval from there, and can be switched off entirely; with it off no timer is created at all, which is the lightest the interface gets. Every colour left empty falls back to the theme, so only what you fill in changes. The ID badge and the UTC stamp are drawn as two layers — a coloured tint over a dark base — and both layers are exposed, so setting the two tints to transparent gives you a flat background. Picking the black-and-white theme still overrides everything, as it should.

The HUD is noticeably lighter on the client. The status loop asked the framework for the full player table five times a second, and because that call crosses the resource boundary it serialised the whole table — inventory and metadata included — on every single tick. Hunger and thirst now read from a cache that qb-core and qbx_core refresh themselves whenever player data changes, so the expensive call happens once at login instead of continuously. Servers whose players carry full inventories will see the biggest difference.

Values that drift constantly — compass heading, engine RPM, vehicle heading, drift angle and aircraft altitude — no longer send a message to the interface on every tick. Each one now has a small threshold and is only sent once it has moved far enough to be visible on screen. This is where the time actually goes in a HUD: every update is a JSON message into the browser process, which costs far more than reading a game native. Speed is deliberately left out of this, since it is the number players actually read.

Two loops that ran every frame — hiding GTA's own HUD components, and blocking the Z key from expanding the radar — were merged into one. Both still run every frame because the natives they use require it, but a frame loop costs something simply by existing, so one loop instead of two removes that overhead outright. With both features switched off in the config, no frame loop is created at all.

The Refresh Rate setting in the menu now applies inside vehicles. The vehicle loop had its interval hard-coded, so a player who chose Low to save frames still received sixteen updates a second while driving — the heaviest loop in the resource was ignoring the one setting meant to control it. Real is unchanged from before; the default now runs at ten updates a second, which is still smooth.

Street name, area and postal code are now looked up on a fixed timer instead of every third tick. Because it counted ticks, choosing the highest refresh rate made these expensive lookups run more than three times as often rather than less, which is the opposite of what that setting is for.

Config.Default entries that quietly did nothing now work: refreshRate, streamerMode, cinematic, postalOnMap, marker3D and focusRP were only ever read from a player's saved settings, so whatever you set in the config was ignored for anyone who had never opened the menu. refreshRate is worth singling out — it happened to match Config.UpdateMs, so the two disagreed silently the moment either one was changed.

Removed Config.Spotify. It was not referenced anywhere in the script, and because config.lua is a shared script it also loads on the client — a clientSecret pasted there would have been shipped to every player who connects.

Database writes are cheaper. Vehicle mileage was written with one query per plate, so eighty cars in traffic meant eighty round trips in a row; it is now a single batched statement, split into chunks. With that in place the write interval was raised from 30 to 180 seconds. Only changed records are ever written, and a clean restart or a player disconnect still writes immediately, so the only exposure is a hard crash — and at most three minutes of mileage.

Fixed the periodic save never running when the database falls back to KVP. The loop sat behind two early exits in the startup thread, so a server without oxmysql — or one where the tables could not be prepared — only saved on player disconnect and on resource stop.

UPGRADING: config.lua is escrow_ignored, so your own file is kept and will not contain the new keys. Nothing breaks without them — Config.Branding simply falls back to the built-in colours and animation, and the old flushInterval of 30 still works, it just writes more often than it needs to now that mileage is batched. To use the new colour options, copy the Config.Branding block over from the new config.lua and raise Config.Database.flushInterval to 180. Config.Spotify can be deleted from your file; it is ignored either way.
